source.text:
One simple problem: new profitable uses for a bank do not automatically make the infrastructure investment profitable.

Of course a CFO can expand the budget. But those opportunities must justify their full costs which include: integration, verification and errors. All of this and generate enough spending at sustainable margins to repay the infrastructure investment.

Ten times the usage at one tenth the price leaves revenue unchanged. Falling costs can improve margins, but the investment case still requires sufficient cash flow over the assets’ useful life.

Even if AI became as important as electricity, it doesn’t follow that today’s buildout will earn adequate returns. Nobody has proven this and the AI infrastructure players are not a representation of that. AI can transform the economy while some infrastructure investments never pay for themselves, both are currently true. The question is whether this scale of spending is justified, not whether AI has a future.

And yes: Nvidia reported $115.8 billion; $96.2 billion was the previous quarter, the article looks to be updated. And that again supports my point: it establishes revenue for the equipment seller, not adequate returns for its buyers or even valuable output. You've also fully discounted the inflated earnings of Nvidia based on outstanding issues: illegal sales to China and a circular financing driven price inflation. And those are just the obvious issues.

You’ve described a mechanism that could justify the spending. You haven’t shown that it will generate enough cash flow, anytime soon, that justifies this buildout. In your electricity analogy, Nvidia is the equipment supplier. Its sales show that companies are buying the infrastructure, that is true. But not that they’ll earn an adequate return from using it. Nvidia getting paid doesn’t mean the buildout pays for itself or somehow makes AI revolutionary as electricity.
